chapter: Early Los Angeles and first bands
title: Los Angeles clubs and musician haunts in the thirties
summary: He describes the drugstore at 43rd and Central, the Bell Tavern and Topsy's, and how many clubs hired piano-and-singer duos.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Was your wife in show business? Because I know that later on she was a showgirl, or was she dancing?

Yes, she was in show business because I met her when I was working, and she used to work at the Cotton Club at the time. And I used to meet her. So all the performers and musicians used to meet at a drugstore at 43rd and Central. You know, when you get off. We had clubs like the Bell Tavern and you know, the ... Topsys -- there was a place called Topsys out on Firestone Boulevard.
Did all of those places have music?

Every one of them. Yeah. They had so many clubs in Los Angeles that had music, you know, during those years, and a lot of them had -- they had piano players and vocalists or piano players and a drummer, you know, some of them, and the drummer would sing or the pianist would sing, and that's when people like Harvey Brooks and Walter Johnson ... I don't know if you've ever heard of Walter Johnson, the pianist, he used to work with a guy -- just the two of them, used to work all over Los Angeles -- just the piano

and a singer -- Johnny Horace. Johnny Horace was his name. They worked every club. L.A. was just loaded with musicians, and clubs and places to play, and really -- remind you, in later years of like, Philadelphia. You know. Los Angeles was what I am speaking of, in the thirties. There were jobs all over town. I don't even know if there were enough musicians to go around.
